title: OCM stakeholders and key influencers
blurb: Recognize who counts as a stakeholder in a change, and spot the key influencers, formal or informal, who shape whether it is adopted.
question: A council is introducing a new app for its street-cleaning crews. Who counts as a stakeholder, and which person is the key influencer most likely to sway the crews?

teach.body: In organizational change management, a stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the change initiative. In plain English: if someone thinks the change touches them, they are a stakeholder, whether or not they are right and whether or not they hold a project role.

teach.h: Three ways to be a stakeholder
head: Test
Example
rows: A depot manager who controls crew rotas
Crews who will use the new app daily
teach.caption: Any one of the three is enough.

teach.body: Key influencers are the people who can shape the perception of the majority within the organizational ecosystem. Through their network, they have the greatest influence on the adoption of the change outcomes and the realization of benefits. They are found by looking at who people listen to and trust, not by reading the organization chart.

teach.caption: Projects involve people with formal roles and key people who hold no formal role (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.1).

teach.h: Is this person a key influencer?

root.label: Do the affected people listen to and trust them?

children.label: A stakeholder, not necessarily an influencer
Supplier or specialist: rarely sways adoption

rows.label: Who
values: Anyone who affects or is affected
Those who shape the majority's view

teach.body: PRINCE2 Project Management asks the project to identify stakeholders and key influencers, recognizing that relationships change over time. Build relationships across interfaces through regular meetings and working groups. Co-creation, which involves users and key influencers in designing products and agreed ways of working, helps those products and ways of working be adopted. Stage boundaries are a good moment to check, because stages often bring new influencers.

Ashcombe District Council is moving its street-cleaning crews to a route-planning app. Project manager Grace Okafor lists the stakeholders: crews, depot managers, residents, the app supplier and the finance team. To find key influencers she asks who crews turn to for advice. The answer is Dev Malhotra, a crew supervisor trusted across all three depots, not the supplier's developer or the finance director. Dev joins the user testing sessions and helps shape the rollout.

teach.text: The key influencer is not automatically the most senior person, the supplier, or the technical expert. It is the person whose network and credibility shape how the affected group sees the change. Also remember: someone who merely perceives themselves to be affected is still a stakeholder.

items: Stakeholder: can affect, be affected by, or perceive itself affected by the change (4.2.2).
Key influencers shape the perception of the majority through their network (4.2.2).
They most influence adoption of change outcomes and realization of benefits.
Key influencers can be formal or informal; many hold no project role.
Relationships change over time; review influencers, for example at stage boundaries.
Co-create products and ways of working with users and key influencers.

summary: You can now recognize stakeholders using the three tests (affect, affected, perceives itself affected). You can also identify key influencers by their network and credibility, formal or informal, and explain why they shape adoption.

A.q: Which statement BEST defines a stakeholder in organizational change management?
options: Anyone holding a formal role within the project management team
Anyone who funds the project and approves its business case
Anyone who can affect, or is or feels affected by, the change
Anyone who signs a contract to supply the project's products
A.why: A stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the change initiative (4.2.2).

whyNot.0: Formal role holders are stakeholders, but so are many people with no role.
whyNot.1: Funders are one kind of stakeholder; the definition is much wider.
whyNot.3: Suppliers are stakeholders, but the definition is not limited to contracts.

A.q: Who are the key influencers in organizational change management?
options: People whose network shapes how the majority sees the change
The most senior managers who sit on the project board for the change
Suppliers who build the products that the change depends on
Specialists who analyse data on the impact of the change
A.why: Key influencers can shape the perception of the majority in the organizational ecosystem and, through their network, most influence adoption and benefits (4.2.2).

whyNot.1: Seniority does not make someone a key influencer; network and credibility do.
whyNot.2: Suppliers rarely sway how the affected majority sees the change.
whyNot.3: Analysts may measure impact, but that does not give them influence over adoption.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or [?] itself to be affected by the change initiative.
options: declare
register
perceive
commit
A.why: The definition includes those who perceive themselves to be affected (4.2.2).

whyNot.0: No declaration is needed to be a stakeholder.
whyNot.1: Being entered in a register is not part of the definition.
whyNot.3: Commitment is not a test of being a stakeholder.

B.q: A council is moving its bin crews to a new routing app. Which person is MOST likely to be a key influencer for crew adoption?
options: The supplier's lead developer who is building the app
The data analyst who will measure route efficiency
The finance director who approved the project budget
A crew supervisor trusted by crews across every depot
B.why: A key influencer is someone whose network shapes the perception of the majority of those affected; the trusted supervisor fits (4.2.2).

whyNot.0: The supplier's developer builds the product but has little sway over the crews.
whyNot.1: An analyst measures impact but is unlikely to shape the crews' view.
whyNot.2: The finance director is a senior stakeholder, not someone the crews look to.

B.q:
Which two statements about OCM stakeholders are correct?
1. Stakeholders can include people with no formal project role.
2. Key influencers are, by definition, members of the project board.
3. Key influencers affect adoption of change outcomes and realization of benefits.
4. People who merely perceive themselves affected are not stakeholders.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Stakeholders include anyone who affects or is (or feels) affected, with or without a role, and key influencers most influence adoption and benefits (4.2.2).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: key influence comes from network and credibility, not board membership.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: board membership does not define influence, and perceived impact counts.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: perceiving itself affected is enough to be a stakeholder.

B.q: Why should a project work with key influencers from the user, supplier and business groups?
options: To replace the need for a communication management approach
To accommodate different views and tailor messages
To pass accountability for the benefits to them
To reduce the number of stakeholders to engage
B.why: Working with key influencers from user, supplier and business groups accommodates different perspectives, strengthens feedback loops and enables tailored messaging (4.4).

whyNot.0: Key influencers support the communication management approach; they do not replace it.
whyNot.2: Accountability for benefits stays with the project executive and the business.
whyNot.3: All stakeholders still need engaging; influencers help reach them.

C.q: A project manager limits engagement to the people named in the role descriptions. Why is this weak?
options: Role descriptions are not produced in agile projects
Stakeholders include people affected who hold no role
Engaging stakeholders is the job of project assurance
Role descriptions list supplier staff rather than users
C.why: Stakeholders include anyone who affects, is affected or perceives itself affected; key people may hold no formal role (4.2.2; PRINCE2 7 3.1).

whyNot.0: Role descriptions are still produced in PRINCE2 Agile, covering the 11 roles.
whyNot.2: Project assurance monitors governance; engaging stakeholders is shared across the team.
whyNot.3: Role descriptions cover all project management team roles, including user-side roles.

C.q: When is a good point to review who the key influencers are, and why?
options: At each daily stand-up, as the team plan changes
When the team dashboard is refreshed each iteration
At stage boundaries, as influencers often change
At closure, once the benefits have been reviewed
C.why: Relationships change over time, and stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.2, 3.5.1).

whyNot.0: Stand-ups coordinate the team's daily work, not stakeholder mapping.
whyNot.1: The team dashboard shows team progress, not the wider influence network.
whyNot.3: Reviewing influencers only at closure is too late to shape adoption.

C.q: A hospital project has identified a respected senior nurse as a key influencer. Which use of this is MOST effective?
options: Appoint her as project executive for the whole project
Ask her to approve the project's tolerance for extra cost
Send her each project dashboard to circulate to colleagues
Involve her in co-creating products and ways of working
C.why: Co-creation involves users and key influencers in designing products and agreed ways of working so they are adopted (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3).

whyNot.0: The project executive is the accountable business role; influence over peers does not make her the right executive.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are set by the business layer and board, not by influencers.
whyNot.2: Project dashboards are pulled, not pushed, and circulating reports is not real engagement.

reteach.title: Who decides what the canteen serves?
reteach.question: If a canteen changes its menu, whose opinion will sway everyone else: the catering director or the colleague everybody lunches with?

blocks.body: Everyone who eats in the canteen is a stakeholder, and so is anyone who thinks the change affects them. But a few people shape what everyone else thinks: the colleague whose opinion people trust. Win them over and the new menu spreads; ignore them and it fails, however senior the sponsor. Those people are key influencers.

blocks.text: The loudest, most senior or most technical person is not automatically the key influencer.

explain.body: A stakeholder can affect the change, is affected by it, or perceives itself to be affected by it. Any one is enough.

test.q: Residents who wrongly believe a new routing app will cancel their collections are:
options: not stakeholders, as their belief is mistaken
key influencers by definition
stakeholders, as they perceive an impact
part of the project management team
test.why: Those who perceive themselves to be affected are stakeholders (4.2.2), whether or not the belief is correct.

whyNot.0: Perceived impact is enough; accuracy does not matter.
whyNot.1: Being worried does not make someone an influencer over the majority.
whyNot.3: Residents hold no project management role.

explain.body: Key influencers shape the perception of the majority within the organizational ecosystem and, through their network, have the greatest influence on adoption and benefits.

options: the time tolerance agreed for each stage
adoption of change outcomes and benefits
the format of the project's dashboards
the order of the processes in the lifecycle
test.why: Key influencers have the greatest influence on the adoption of the change outcomes and the realization of benefits (4.2.2).

whyNot.0: Time tolerance is set through governance, not by influencers.
whyNot.2: Dashboards are co-created by teams and the project manager.
whyNot.3: The process order is set by the method, not by influencers.

explain.body: Projects involve people with formal roles and key people who are impacted or critical to success but hold no formal role. Influence comes from trust and networks.

test.q: Can a key influencer hold no formal role in the project?
options: Yes, influence comes from network and trust
No, they must sit on the project board
No, they must be named in the role descriptions
Yes, once the supplier has agreed to it
test.why: Key influencers are defined by their network and ability to shape the majority's perception, not by role (4.2.2).

whyNot.1: Board membership is not part of the definition.
whyNot.2: Many key influencers appear in no role description.
whyNot.3: No supplier agreement is involved in being an influencer.

explain.body: Stakeholder relationships change over time, so engagement is revisited. Stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships.

test.q: Stakeholder relationships during a project are:
options: set once the project brief is approved
reviewed at closure when writing the lessons report
managed by the supplier's account team
likely to change, so engagement is revisited
test.why: Relationships change over time, so stakeholders and key influencers are reviewed as the project progresses (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Relationships keep shifting after the brief is approved.
whyNot.1: Waiting for closure misses the chance to act on changes.
whyNot.2: Engagement is the project's job, not the supplier's sales team.
